GE’s petition for review is granted because the EPA promulgated a 
legislative rule without following the procedures required by the TSCA and 
the APA. The Guidance Document is accordingly vacated.
No t e s
1. 
Policy Statements and Finality. In General Electric, the D.C. Circuit 
directly answers the question of whether the guidance at issue constitutes a 
legislative rule or poUcy statement. Suits challenging purported policy 
statements for being disguised legislative rules often confront an additional 
question—^whether the agency’s issuance of the guidance is “final” under the 
APA and therefore subject to judicial review—but this question generally 
tracks the question of whether the guidance is a legislative rule or pohcy 
statement. In National Mining Association v. McCarthy, 758 F.3d 243, 250—51 
(D.C. Cir. 2014), the court stated expressly that a genuine policy statement, 
prior to enforcement, can never be “final” and thus subject to judicial review. 
For further discussion of finality, see Chapter 8.
2. 
When Are Agency Statements Binding"^ General Electric says a 
purported pohcy statement may be a legislative rule if it “has binding effects 
on private parties or on the agency.” How can judges operationahze this 
principle? General Electric focuses largely on the text of the purported pohcy 
statement itself, the close reading of documents being a task weh within the 
judicial comfort zone. But General Electric suggests that EPA might have 
overcome the inference of binding effect from the face of the document had it 
cited contrary evidence from the document’s apphcation. What might that 
evidence have looked like? Cf. Catawba County, North Carolina v. EPA, 571 
F.3d 20, 33—34 (D.C. Cir. 2009) (finding an EPA memorandum to be non-
binding on its face but also citing actual departures by EPA from the terms of 
the memorandum in specific instances as further evidence of its non-binding 
nature). And if a purported pohcy statement were not binding on its face, could 
evidence of its apphcation—or of private parties’ comphance with it—^be 
sufficient, by itself, to make the statement a legislative rule? In Appalachian 
Power, the D.C. Circuit confronted an EPA paper entitled ‘Teriodic Monitoring 
Guidance” whose last paragraph stated: “The pohcies set forth in this paper 
are intended solely as guidance, do not represent final agency action, and 
cannot be rehed upon to create any rights enforceable by any party.” The court
